system.name: mRPC
system.one_liner: an RPC framework that runs marshalling and policy enforcement as a single privileged, managed system service instead of a library plus sidecar

components.name: App
components.role: the application issuing and receiving RPC calls

components.name: RPC Library
components.role: linked-in library that marshals RPC parameters (current approach)

components.name: Sidecar
components.role: separate process that mediates network traffic and applies policies (current approach)

components.name: Policies
components.role: policy logic run inside the sidecar

components.name: mRPC Library
components.role: lightweight library apps link against in the proposed design

components.name: mRPC
components.role: privileged, trusted system service that performs marshalling after policy processing

components.name: Frontend Engine
components.role: part of the mRPC service that routes RPCs and applies flexible processing logic

components.name: Transport Engine
components.role: part of the mRPC service that handles the transport backend (e.g. RDMA/TCP)

components.name: Flexible RPC Processing Logic
components.role: pluggable policy/transport modules such as rate limiting, ACL, RDMA, TCP

components.name: Kernel
components.role: OS kernel network stack traversed by both designs

flows.what: RPC Call, marshalled/unmarshalled (M/U) at each hop

RPC data processed by the managed service instead of an app-linked sidecar

content.key_idea: Collapsing the app-linked RPC library and the separate policy-enforcing sidecar into one privileged mRPC service cuts the number of (un)marshalling steps from 12 to 4 while still centrally enforcing policy.
content.reading_order: left panel (a) top-to-bottom shows the current library+sidecar design and its Call/Reply marshal/unmarshal trace; right panel (b) shows the proposed mRPC design and its shorter trace, inviting direct visual comparison of the two.

evidence: The typical architecture is to enforce policies in a sidecar—a separate process that mediates the network traffic
we combine them into a single privilege and trusted sys- tem service (Figure 1b)
Using a sidecar triples the number of (un)marshalling steps (from 4 to 12)

summary: This figure compares two RPC architectures side by side. Panel (a), 'Now: Library+Sidecar', shows an app linked with an RPC library that marshals data, plus a separate sidecar process that unmarshals, applies policies, and re-marshals traffic before it reaches the kernel and NIC; the Call/Reply trace at the bottom shows 12 marshal/unmarshal (M/U) operations. Panel (b), 'Our Vision: RPC as a Managed Service', shows the app linked with a thin mRPC library talking to a single privileged mRPC service containing a Frontend Engine, Transport Engine, and pluggable Flexible RPC Processing Logic (rate limiting, ACL, RDMA, TCP); its trace shows only 4 M/U operations. The figure argues visually that merging marshalling and policy enforcement into one service removes redundant data copies and marshalling steps while retaining the sidecar's flexible policy control.
summary_zh: 该图对比两种RPC架构：(a)当前的库+边车方案，App库与Sidecar分别封送数据，Call/Reply路径上共12次封送/解封送；(b)提出的mRPC托管服务方案，将封送与策略执行合并进单一特权服务，路径上仅4次操作。
